analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax with a flat 20% tax on wages and business profits.
analysis.headline: The 20% flat-tax bill, introduced June 7, 1995 with 7 Republican cosponsors, never left the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 104th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would scrap the existing income tax and replace it with a single 20% tax on wages, salaries, and business profits. Only earned income — paychecks — would be taxed at the individual level, so dividends, interest, capital gains, and rental income would no longer be taxed at all. Families would get a bigger standard deduction with $4,500 per dependent, but nearly all other deductions except charity and home-mortgage interest would disappear.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners with large investment income would gain the most, since money from wealth would no longer be taxed at all and the top rate on wages would drop to 20%. Large working families with modest wages would also gain, because the standard deduction grows and each dependent subtracts $4,500 from taxable income. Profitable, capital-intensive businesses would pay 20% on business cash flow with immediate write-offs for equipment and buildings, instead of corporate rates up to 35%.

how_it_helps.text: Taxes individuals only on earned income, so dividends, interest, capital gains, and rents would carry a 0% individual tax rate — the largest dollar gains go to households living on investment wealth.
Cuts the individual rate to a flat 20%, well below the top rates high-earning wage earners faced under the 1995 code.

Gives working families a larger standard deduction — $16,500 for a married couple, $9,500 for a single filer, plus $4,500 per dependent, adjusted for inflation — so a family of four would owe nothing on roughly its first $25,500 of wages.

Replaces the corporate tax with a 20% tax on business taxable income after full deduction of purchases, wages, and investment in property, letting businesses write off equipment and buildings immediately; the tax applies to all business owners, not just corporations.

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners as a group would bear the entire individual tax, since income from wealth escapes tax while paychecks are taxed at 20% with no lower brackets. Itemizers who depend on deductions the bill drops — state and local taxes, medical expenses — could pay more than under current law. Homeowners with mortgages above the new $100,000 cap would lose part of their interest deduction, and employee fringe benefits other than retirement plans would no longer be deductible for businesses. Cutting the tax base this way would also mean less federal revenue, requiring offsetting taxes elsewhere or spending cuts.

drawbacks.text: By taxing only earned income, the bill shifts the tax burden off investment wealth and onto work: a retiree or investor with large dividends and capital gains would pay nothing, while a worker with the same income pays 20%.

Families could deduct almost nothing beyond the standard deduction, charitable gifts, and home-mortgage interest — state and local taxes and medical expenses would no longer count, so many middle-income itemizers would see their taxes rise.

The home-mortgage interest deduction would be cut sharply, limited to acquisition debt of $100,000 (down from $1,000,000) and home-equity debt of $50,000 (down from $500,000), raising costs for homeowners with larger mortgages.
A 20% flat rate on a base that excludes investment income would collect substantially less than the tax code it replaces, forcing either higher taxes elsewhere or cuts to federal programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would genuinely simplify taxes and would zero out tax bills for many working families with children, which is a real gain. But its dominant effect is to move the tax burden off wealth and onto wages: the biggest winners are high earners with substantial portfolios, who would pay 20% on wages and nothing on investment income, while middle-income itemizers could pay more. As designed, the benefits skew heavily toward those already at the top, and the loss of deductions would hit many ordinary taxpayers harder than the lower rate helps them.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the Congress and expired when the session ended, never reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Representative Souder introduced the flat-tax bill on June 7, 1995, with six colleagues joining as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote after the referral.
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with only its seven Republican cosponsors and no floor action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, wage earners who would have shouldered the shifted tax burden — and itemizers who would have lost their state, local, and medical deductions — are no worse off. The Ways and Means chairman also kept control of tax policy for his own overhaul plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners who would have paid more

for.name: Rep. Mark Souder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat-tax bill on June 7, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 7 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Solomon, Doolittle, Baker of California, Foley, and Barton of Texas as original cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; the committee took up his own tax-overhaul proposal instead, and H.R. 1780 died without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll call exists; the bill's only recorded supporters were its eight Republican sponsors, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill taxes only earned income, so dividends, interest, capital gains, and rents would face a 0% individual tax rate. Their gain comes directly at the expense of wage earners, who would carry the entire individual tax.

Businesses would pay a 20% tax on business cash flow with immediate expensing of equipment and property, replacing corporate rates that ran up to 35% — a large cut for profitable, capital-intensive firms. The main offset is that fringe benefits other than retirement contributions would no longer be deductible.

The mortgage-interest deduction — the housing industry's core tax subsidy — would survive, but its cap would fall from $1 million to $100,000 of acquisition debt, shrinking demand at the high end of the market.
The charitable deduction would be preserved as one of only three individual deductions, keeping the tax incentive that supports charitable giving.
Eliminating the deduction for state and local taxes would make it costlier for residents to pay state and local taxes, squeezing the finances of high-tax states and cities.
